core: Metabolism as all the physical and chemical processes in the body that convert or use energy (working definition, attributed to MedlinePlus)
The everyday processes metabolism covers: breathing, circulation, body-temperature control, muscle contraction, digestion, waste removal, brain and nerve function

Anabolism (building and storing; small building blocks assembled into larger molecules) and catabolism (breaking large molecules down to release energy, producing waste), each with an original example
The body burns fuel from food for its daily work, the general picture (calorie specifics owned by energy-and-calories)
Metabolic rate as how fast the body uses energy; basal metabolic rate (BMR) as the resting baseline
What affects metabolic rate: age, body size, body composition (muscle vs fat), activity, and genes — stated factually, with no weight-loss advice
Metabolism and food: digestion yields glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids that cells use as energy or store for later
Honest framing: metabolism is steady, continuous work, not a switch that foods can flip on or off
supporting: Enzymes are the proteins that speed up and control metabolic reactions
Thousands of metabolic reactions run at the same time
After a meal the balance of activity tilts toward anabolism
Metabolic breakdown produces waste products removed via skin, kidneys, lungs, and intestines
outOfScope: Calorie math, calorie values of foods, and energy expenditure figures (energy-and-calories topic)
Energy balance and how the body gains or loses weight (energy-balance topic)
Biochemical pathway detail, named enzyme chemistry, and hormone mechanisms (biology subject)

claims.claim: Metabolism refers to all the physical and chemical processes in the body that convert or use energy, including breathing, circulating blood, controlling body temperature, contracting muscles, digesting food and nutrients, eliminating waste, and the functioning of the brain and nerves.

Anabolism is the building-and-storing side of metabolism: small building blocks (such as amino acids) are assembled into larger, more complex molecules (such as muscle protein), and energy is stored for later.

Catabolism is the breaking-down side of metabolism: cells break large molecules (mostly carbohydrates and fats) apart to release energy, which fuels anabolism, warms the body, and powers muscle contraction; the breakdown also produces waste products.
Basal metabolic rate (BMR) measures how quickly the body burns energy while at rest; it is the pace of the body's idle metabolic work.

Metabolic rate is affected by age (it generally slows as people get older), body composition (more muscle and less fat generally means a higher resting rate, because muscle burns more energy at rest than fat), activity, body size, and genes.

Food supplies metabolism's fuel and building blocks: digestion breaks carbohydrates into simple sugars such as glucose, proteins into amino acids, and fats into fatty acids; the blood carries these to cells, which use them for energy or store them (especially in the liver, muscles, and body fat).
Metabolism is continuous steady work: thousands of metabolic reactions happen at the same time to keep cells healthy and working, and the body's energy use at rest continues even during sleep.

Federal health agencies treat the body's use of energy from food as the scientific basis for understanding weight and nutrition, with no 'switch' that special products can flip; the NIH's NIDDK presents weight management as grounded in that science.

conflictingEvidence: No conflicts among the cited sources on the core claims; MedlinePlus and Nemours KidsHealth agree on the definition, the anabolism/catabolism split, BMR, and the age/body-composition/activity factors. Note: OpenStax Nutrition was restructured (2024, now 'Nutrition for Nurses') and its canonical energy-balance chapter from the phase guidance is no longer present at the expected URL, so this topic relies on MedlinePlus and KidsHealth for the Tier A/B coverage. Popular claims that specific foods 'boost' or 'reset' metabolism are unsupported by these sources and are addressed by the honest-framing section.
unsupportedExistingClaims: Popular claims that particular foods, drinks, or supplements can dramatically 'boost' or 'reset' metabolism are not supported by the cited sources and are contradicted by the steady-work framing used here.
